theme: Israel demands a king; Saul anointed, God as true King
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 8:1-10:27. Israel asks for a king, and Saul is chosen. This is one of the most important turning points in the Old Testament. Read the elders’ request, and listen for what it reveals about their hearts.
settingTheScene: Samuel is old, and his sons are corrupt. The elders of Israel gather at Ramah and ask for a king “to judge us like all the nations.” Samuel is displeased, and God tells him that the people have not rejected Samuel, but God. The following chapters describe how Saul, a young Benjaminite, is found, anointed in private by Samuel, and presented publicly at Mizpah. The monarchy begins, with a mixture of divine permission and human error.
observation: The elders say, “Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations” (8:5).
The LORD says, “They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them” (8:7).
Samuel warns them what a king will take: sons, daughters, fields, and servants (8:10-18).
The people refuse to listen: “No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations” (8:19-20).
Saul is described as “a handsome young man… from his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people” (9:2).
Saul is searching for lost donkeys and finds Samuel, who anoints him privately (9:3-10:1).
The Spirit of God rushes on Saul, and he prophesies (10:6-13).
At Mizpah, Saul is chosen by lot but is found hiding among the baggage (10:17-24).
interpretation:
The request for a king is not simply wrong. The law of Moses had anticipated it (Deuteronomy 17:14-20), and God had promised kings from Judah (Genesis 49:10). What is wrong is the reason. The elders want a king “like all the nations.” Israel was supposed to be different. Their distinctiveness was that the LORD was their king. Wanting to be like the nations is a form of unbelief, a desire to trust in visible power instead of the invisible God.

Samuel’s warning is a catalog of what human kings do: take. The word appears again and again. A king will take your sons for his army, your daughters for his kitchen, your best fields, your servants, and a tenth of your flocks. “And you shall be his slaves.” It is a prophecy of Solomon’s oppression and of every oppressive government. Yet the people say no, they will have a king. God gives them what they ask, and what they ask for will cost them.

Saul looks like a king. He is tall and handsome. But the narrative also shows his weaknesses. He is searching for lost donkeys, he is shy, and when he is chosen, he hides among the baggage. His humility is attractive, but it will turn into insecurity and fear of the people. At this stage, though, the Spirit of the LORD comes on him, and “God gave him another heart” (10:9). He begins well.

The chapters show a delicate balance. The monarchy is permitted, even blessed, and yet it is the fruit of a flawed motive. God works through human weakness. He will take Israel’s misguided desire for a king and, in time, produce the king who is the Messiah. The people wanted a king like the nations. God will give them a king who is nothing like the nations.
connection: Jesus is the king who does not take but gives, who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” (John 18:33), and he answered, “My kingdom is not of this world.” The people shouted, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), echoing the elders’ rejection of God. Revelation 19:16 shows him as King of kings.
application:
Ask where you are tempted to follow what everyone else does instead of trusting God.

Think about who or what you rely on in place of God, and what it costs you.

Thank God that Jesus is a king who gives himself for his people.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have wanted to be like the nations.
Ask him to keep you from trusting anything visible more than him.
Thank Jesus, the king who serves.
